The Proximal Operator as a Piecewise Linear Table

Source: R/prox_spec.R
penalty_prox_spec.Rd

Returns the scalar proximal operator of a separable penalty as an odd piecewise linear map: three matrices of cuts, slopes and intercepts from which a compiled loop can apply the operator without reference to the family. Returns NULL for a penalty whose operator has no such description; where such a penalty has an operator, it is applied with penalty_prox().

Usage

penalty_prox_spec(pen, theta, step, ...)

Arguments

pen

A penalty() object of any branch.

theta

A named list of hyperparameter values, or a named numeric vector carrying the same, holding every name in pen@params.

step

A numeric vector of step lengths, either a single value used for every coefficient or one value per coefficient. Every entry must be finite and positive, and any other length or value is rejected with an error naming step.

...

Passed to methods. The shipped methods do not read it.

Value

A list of three matrices, cut, slope and icept, each with pen@n_coef rows and one column per piece. The last column of cut is Inf. The value is NULL where the operator has no piecewise linear description.

The piecewise linear map

The operator of a separable penalty acts one coordinate at a time and is odd, so it is determined by its action on \(\lvert u\rvert\): on the \(k\)-th interval, the first for which \(\lvert u\rvert \le\) cut[j, k],

$$\mathrm{prox}(u) = \mathrm{sign}(u)\,(a_{jk}\lvert u\rvert + b_{jk}),$$

with \(a_{jk}\) = slope[j, k] and \(b_{jk}\) = icept[j, k]. Every closed-form operator of a separable penalty in the package has this shape. The table below is for a step of 0.5, with \(\sigma = 0.8\) for the Gaussian prior (whose single cut does not depend on \(\sigma\)), \(\lambda = 1.5\) for the Laplace prior, \(\lambda = 1.5\) and \(\alpha = 0.6\) for the elastic net, \(\lambda = 1\) and \(\gamma = 3\) for MCP, and \(\lambda = 1\) and \(a = 3.7\) for SCAD:

penaltypiecescuts
Gaussian prior (gaussian1 parent)1Inf
Laplace prior (lasso_penalty())20.75, Inf
elastic net (elasticnet_penalty())20.45, Inf
MCP30.5, 3, Inf
SCAD40.5, 1.5, 3.7, Inf

The last cut is always Inf. prox_apply() evaluates a table, and the tests of the package compare it with penalty_prox() at every cut, on both sides of every cut and over a grid of points.

Accuracy near the step limit of SCAD and MCP

The table of SCAD and MCP is ill-conditioned as the step approaches its limit, \(a - 1\) for SCAD and \(\gamma\) for MCP. On the tapering piece the slope is \(1/(1 - t/(a-1))\) for SCAD and \(1/(1 - t/\gamma)\) for MCP, which grows without bound as the step approaches the limit, and the intercept grows with it and has the opposite sign, so \(a_{jk}\lvert u\rvert + b_{jk}\) is the difference of two large numbers that nearly cancel. The table is therefore less accurate there than penalty_prox(), which evaluates the same piece in a form without this cancellation. With a curvature or a diagonal map the limit applies to the scaled step \(t_j c_j d_j^2\) described below.

Why a table rather than the operator

A coordinate descent applies the operator once per coordinate per sweep, at a point that moves every time, so a compiled loop that called back into R for each application would lose the speed gained by compiling it. Passing the numbers keeps the loop compiled. The table holds the mathematics of the penalty, and the compiled kernel evaluates any map of this shape without reference to the family.

Why the step is a vector

In a coordinate descent the step of coordinate \(j\) is \(1/v_j\) with \(v_j = \sum_i w_i x_{ij}^2\), which does not change while the working weights are held fixed. The whole table is therefore built once per weighted least squares iteration and read by every sweep. penalty_prox(), by contrast, takes a single step.

Under a diagonal map

Standardization is a diagonal \(D\), under which a separable penalty stays separable and the table is still available. The builder is called at the step \(t_j d_j^2\), and the cuts and intercepts that it returns are divided by \(\lvert d_j\rvert\), while the slopes are unchanged because each slope multiplies a point that was scaled and then divided back. The operator is odd, so only the magnitude of \(d\) enters. For a lasso the cut is \(t_j \lvert d_j\rvert \lambda\) (with \(d = (0.5, 2, 3)\), \(t = 0.4\) and \(\lambda = 1.2\) the cuts are 0.24, 0.96 and 1.44).

The step limit of SCAD and MCP is tested on the scaled step. With \(c_j\) the curvature of the coordinate (the curv property, one when it is empty), the table exists only while \(t_j c_j d_j^2 < a - 1\) for SCAD and \(t_j c_j d_j^2 < \gamma\) for MCP in every coordinate, so a standardized penalty takes shorter steps.

A diagonal map is recognized by its class through map_diagonal(). distrib_penalty() (and therefore lasso_penalty() and elasticnet_penalty()), scad_penalty() and mcp_penalty() store a square map whose off-diagonal entries are all zero as a Matrix::Diagonal() object, so a diagonal base matrix gives a table. A diagonal map with a zero entry gives NULL.

Penalties without a table

NULL is returned for a quadratic or structured penalty, whose operator is one linear solve over every coordinate at once, and for an additive penalty. Among separable penalties, NULL is returned under a map that is not recognized as diagonal, which is the generalized-lasso problem; for a parent read blockwise, whose coordinates do not separate; for a parent other than the Gaussian, Laplace and elastic-net families, whose operator has no closed form (the Student t prior, for example, has an operator computed by root finding); for a parent whose gradient at zero is not zero, that is, a parent not centered at zero; and for SCAD or MCP when the scaled step \(t_j c_j d_j^2\) of some coordinate reaches \(a - 1\) or \(\gamma\), where the operator is set-valued.

See also

prox_apply() to evaluate the table, penalty_prox() for the operator itself, has_prox() for whether there is one at all, spec_diag() for the diagonal-map transport.

Examples

# A lasso at two different steps: the threshold is t * lambda.
pen <- lasso_penalty(n_coef = 2L)
sp <- penalty_prox_spec(pen, list(lambda = 1.5), step = c(0.5, 2))
sp$cut
#>      [,1] [,2]
#> [1,] 0.75  Inf
#> [2,] 3.00  Inf

# The table reproduces the operator. The first point lies on its cut and
# is set to zero; the second is shrunk by t * lambda.
u <- c(0.75, 4)
prox_apply(sp, u)
#> [1] 0 1
c(penalty_prox(lasso_penalty(n_coef = 1), u[1], 0.5, list(lambda = 1.5)),
  penalty_prox(lasso_penalty(n_coef = 1), u[2], 2, list(lambda = 1.5)))
#> [1] 0 1

# SCAD has four pieces, and no table at a step where its operator is
# set-valued.
penalty_prox_spec(scad_penalty(), list(lambda = 1, a = 3.7),
                  step = 0.5)$cut
#>      [,1] [,2] [,3] [,4]
#> [1,]  0.5  1.5  3.7  Inf
penalty_prox_spec(scad_penalty(), list(lambda = 1, a = 3.7), step = 2.7)
#> NULL

# A quadratic penalty has a solve, not a coordinatewise map.
penalty_prox_spec(quadratic_penalty(diag(2)), list(lambda = 1), step = 0.5)
#> NULL
